html.k04: A fine needle aspiration takes a few cells from a lump in your thyroid, so a pathologist can look at them under a microscope and work out what the lump is. This page explains what it is, what happens on the day, what you'll feel, and what comes after.
html.k05: In a hurry? The whole thing in five lines
html.k06: A lump in your thyroid needs checking, and a scan alone can't say what it is.
html.k07: A very fine needle takes a few cells from the lump, guided by ultrasound.
html.k08: You lie back with your neck gently extended. It usually takes approximately 30 minutes.
html.k09: The needle goes in and out a few times. Most people find it quicker and less uncomfortable than they expected.
html.k10: You go home the same day. Results usually take about 2 weeks, and you should come back for the follow-up appointment.
html.k11: A thyroid nodule is an abnormal growth of thyroid cells into a lump inside your thyroid. The thyroid is a gland at the front of your neck, below your voice box, that makes hormones controlling how your body uses energy.
html.k12: Most thyroid nodules are benign — that means non-cancerous. But some can be cancerous, and no one can tell just by looking at your neck. That is why your doctor has asked for this test.
html.k13: The purpose of the FNAC is to find out the nature of the nodule and to try to rule out the possibility of cancer in your thyroid gland.
html.k14: FNAC is the standard first test for this. It gives your doctor real information — enough to decide whether you need treatment, further tests, or simply to be monitored.
html.k15: Tap any step below, or press play, to watch what happens. You can drag the picture to rotate it, and pause at any point.
html.k21: This is what people worry about most, so here it is honestly:
html.k22: Pressure on your neck from the ultrasound probe resting there.
html.k23: A slight pin prick from the needle. It is finer than the needle used for a routine blood test.
html.k24: Some pressure as the samples are taken.
html.k25: You may feel very little. Most people describe it as quick, and less uncomfortable than they expected.
html.k26: You'll be asked to stay as still as you can and to avoid coughing, talking or swallowing while the needle is in, because those movements shift the thyroid and make accurate placement harder.
html.k27: The procedure is done by inserting a fine needle into the nodule and making several passes to obtain a small sample of tissue, which is sent to the laboratory for evaluation.
html.k28: It is carried out under ultrasound guidance so the needle is placed accurately — using the same scanning that found the nodule.
html.k29: You will usually be offered a local anaesthetic injection to numb the site. It is optional, but it is commonly given.
html.k31: Tell your doctor if you are on any blood thinners or antiplatelets — medicines such as warfarin, rivaroxaban, aspirin or clopidogrel. Tell them before the procedure, and do not stop any of these on your own. Your doctor will say whether any should be paused, and when to restart them.
html.k32: FNAC is generally safe. Minor effects such as slight pain, bruising or swelling are common but usually settle quickly; serious complications are rare. These are the risks your doctor wants you to know about:
html.k36: The results usually take about 2 weeks to process. Your primary doctor will arrange to tell you the results.
html.k37: If anything here is unclear or worrying, ask your doctor. Bring this page with you — it is easier to talk it through together.
html.k40: Fine, slightly thinner than a blood-taking needle
html.k42: Thyroid nodules are common, and most are benign. Most people with one are simply monitored, but a small number need further tests or treatment — that is what the FNAC is checking.
html.k47: Tell your doctor about any blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines you take.
html.k48: You do not normally need to stop eating or drinking beforehand.
html.k49: Wear something comfortable that lets your neck be reached easily.
html.k50: Write down your questions — nothing is too small to ask.
html.k52: In up to about 20% of cases not enough cells are sampled for the pathologist to make a clear diagnosis.
html.k53: From bleeding. It is exceptionally rare for bleeding to cause this — but it is why you must seek help if it happens.
html.k54: Up to about 20% of FNAC results may return as non-diagnostic or inadequate, because not enough cells were sampled for the pathologist to make a clear diagnosis. If this happens, the usual next step is to repeat the test — another small sample is taken — and your doctor will discuss whether any further tests are needed.
html.k55: These complications are not intended to be exhaustive and may vary depending on underlying medical condition. They are NOT meant to be, and CANNOT be, exhaustive.
html.k56: A non-diagnostic result does not mean something is wrong. It means there were not enough cells to be certain; the test is usually repeated, and your doctor will discuss what to do next.
html.k57: Leave the adhesive dressing over the puncture site in place. After that it can be removed, and the area washed if you want to.
html.k58: You can go back to usual, non-strenuous activities, including eating and drinking.
html.k59: Avoid strenuous activity — heavy lifting or contact sports.
html.k60: Slight pain, swelling or bruising at the site can be eased with simple painkillers such as Panadol.
html.k61: You have a sudden increase in pain or swelling, continued bleeding, or difficulty breathing.
html.k62: It is important to attend the follow-up appointment so the results can be discussed properly with you. Waiting can feel long — that is normal, and the wait itself does not mean anything has gone wrong.
html.k63: If you are not keen for FNAC, your doctor will not be able to determine the nature of the nodule and to rule out the possibility of cancer within the thyroid gland. You should discuss alternative options for managing your thyroid nodule with your doctor, e.g. monitoring the nodule with regular ultrasound or excision biopsy of the nodule for histology. These options would be best discussed with your primary (referring) doctor.
html.k64: There is a chance that the nodule will turn out to be cancerous and you risk missing the necessary treatment.

step01.n: This is the front of your neck, below the jaw. Inside is the thyroid, a small gland that sits over the windpipe. Nothing here is to scale with anything scary. It is just your neck.

step02.n: The lump your doctor wants to test is a nodule inside the thyroid. Nodules are common and most are not cancer, but a small sample is taken so it can be checked.

step03.n: The skin over the lump is cleaned and the area is covered with a sterile drape. That is all this step involves, and it takes a moment.

step04.n: The doctor rests the ultrasound probe on the front of your neck. It shows the lump on a screen, so its exact position and depth are known before anything else happens.

step05.n: The needle is lined up at an angle just under the probe, so that it can reach the lump without touching anything it should not.

step06.n: A very fine, thin needle passes through the skin and into the lump. It is usually a quick, sharp scratch that lasts a moment. This is why the doctor keeps the probe in place while watching the screen.

step07.n: Inside the lump the needle moves gently back and forth for a few seconds to collect cells. You may feel some pressure while this is happening. A few passes are made, depending on whether there are enough cells.

step08.n: The needle is removed and gentle pressure is held on the spot for a moment. Any discomfort settles quickly. The sample of cells goes to the laboratory.

step09.n: A small dressing is placed over the spot. You can usually go home shortly afterwards. You can eat, drink and shower as normal, and carry on with your usual activities. Mild tenderness or a little bruising for a day or two is normal. Results usually take about two weeks.
